question: We are writing following continued discussions on whether linear and logistic regression models may be classified as AI systems under the AI Act. These models have been widely used in financial services for decades, are generally explainable and already subject to extensive financial services, consumer protection and data protection rules.

Classifying linear and logistic regression models as AI would extend the scope of the AI Act to established statistical methods that do not carry the same risks, creating additional compliance and supervisory burdens without clear benefits. The Commission’s June 2025 Guidelines indicate that linear and logistic regression models fall outside the definition of an AI system.

This is consistent with the positions taken by the European Central Bank and the European Insurance and Occupational Pensions Authority, the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD) approach with which the AI Act is aligned and the view supported by Member States in the AI Board subgroup on financial services.
How will the Commission ensure that any future guidance remains consistent with its guidelines, established supervisory practice and the OECD approach?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (17.9.2026) Article 3(1) of the AI Act1 defines an AI system in a manner aligned with the approach of the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development. Recital 12 of the AI Act clarifies that techniques that enable inference while building an AI system include machine learning (ML) approaches that learn from data how to achieve certain objectives.

Systems based on linear or logistic regression use ML techniques. Their parameters are learned from their training data. The Commission considers these systems to fall outside the definition of an AI system where they meet the narrow conditions outlined in points 42 to 45 of the Guidelines on the AI system definition2.

If such systems permit adjustments of their decision-making models in an intelligent way, they fall within that definition. For the financial sector, the AI Act classifies as high-risk AI systems that fall within the two use cases listed in point 5(b) and (c) of Annex III of the AI Act3.

Such systems are subject to requirements under the AI Act regarding, inter alia, their design and use to mitigate potential risks to fundamental rights4. Nevertheless, no high-risk AI system placed on the market5 before 2 December 2027 will be subject to these requirements unless its design is significantly changed after this date.

The Commission´s public consultation6 on the draft guidelines on the classification of highrisk AI systems included specific questions on the need to remove, adapt or add high-risk use cases to the list in Annex III of the AI Act. Findings will be published in a report pursuant to Article 112(1) of the AI Act.

The Commission is working towards a simplified and proportionate approach for the application of the AI Act’s requirements to high-risk AI systems based on linear or logistic regression used in the financial sector that properly reflects those systems’ transparent and explainable nature.
1 Regulation (EU) 2024/1689. 2 C(2025) 5053 final. 3 That classification has been done even if the use cases in practice largely relied on systems based on linear or

logistic regression given their dependency on data and risks of biases. 4 In particular the right to non-discrimination, especially when trained on biased data sets. 5 The same applies to high-risk AI systems put into service before 2 December 2027. 6 https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/consultations/targeted-consultation-draft-guidelines-classification-highrisk-artificial-intelligence-systems.
